finite_matrix_derivations.derivation: Cij=A_j A_i gives Cji*=Cij. For block u, Cauchy–Schwarz on sum_ij <A_j u_i,A_i u_j> gives |u*Cu|<=sum_j u_j*(sum_i A_i^2)u_j<=sigma^2||u||^2. Regrouping via B_a=sum_i (u_i)_a A_i gives |u*Cu|<=sum_a||B_a||_F^2<=v^2||u||^2. Thus the stronger absolute norm estimate in the card is valid. A diagonal compression A_i^2 gives lambda_max(C)>=0; commuting coefficients make C=R*R and ||R||^2=sigma^2. Identity tensor amplification preserves the spectrum up to repetition.
finite_matrix_derivations.category_decision: Moved from matrix-trace to matrix-spectral: the claim is a deterministic block-matrix spectral-norm/eigenvalue comparison, not primarily a trace inequality or matrix-function theorem.

finite_matrix_derivations.derivation: The Hermite degree-p space has dimension binomial(s+p,p). The raising map L_p has L_p*L_p bounded by [sigma^2+(p-1)kappa^2]I, using the commutator and C<=kappa^2 I. X_p=L_p+L_p* then has norm at most twice that root. X^p applied to each vacuum basis vector never reaches degree above p, giving exactly E tr_d X^(2p)=d^-1 sum_j ||X_p^p(e_j tensor 1)||^2. Jensen adds d^(1/(2p)) for the spectral norm. For d>=2 and kappa>0, let ell=log(2d) and p=ceil(ell+sigma sqrt(ell)/kappa). Since kappa<=sigma and ell>1, sigma^2+p kappa^2<=(sigma+kappa sqrt(ell))^2 and d^(1/(2p))<=1+ell/p, giving 2sigma+4kappa sqrt(log(2d))<=2sigma+6kappa sqrt(log d). For kappa=0 every coefficient vanishes; for d=1 the scalar absolute-Gaussian mean is sqrt(2/pi)sigma.
finite_matrix_derivations.boundary_checks: p is an integer at least 1, the trace is normalized, d=1 is separate, and no limit of finite-degree operators is asserted. In particular X_p^(2p) on arbitrary vectors is not substituted for the full multiplication operator.

finite_matrix_derivations.derivation: The Fourier coefficient map F_(pi,i,j),g=sqrt(d_pi/N)pi(g)_ij is square because sum d_pi^2=N and unitary by Schur orthogonality. For z=xi+i eta with independent standard real coordinates, Ezz*=2I and Ezz^T=0, both preserved by unitary F; realification is an orthogonal map on 2N real Gaussian coordinates. Thus all output coordinates are independent circular Gaussians. The regular representation is the direct sum of I_dpi tensor pi, giving the stated block scaling and maximum norm.
finite_matrix_derivations.boundary_checks: For real input coefficients, Fourier covariance Eww*=I does not by itself imply independent complex coordinates: pseudocovariance can be nonzero. In an abelian group, conjugate characters give conjugate random Fourier coordinates. The card correctly excludes that false extension.

finite_matrix_derivations.derivation: For subset S of size m, unitary coefficients give sigma^2=m. Schur orthogonality gives full entry covariance (N/d_pi)I and the subset covariance is smaller in Loewner order; weak variance is at most m. Below q^4, q=eN/m, NCK gives O(sqrt(m log q)); above q^4, the intrinsic-freeness correction is sqrt(m)[(log(d)^3/d)(N/m)]^(1/4)=O(sqrt(m)), since log(d)^3/d decreases for d>e^3 and q>=e. Gaussian Lipschitz tails are at most q^-C3. Since |Sigma|<=N, the Gaussian correlation inequality yields joint mass >=exp(-2 sum p_pi)>=exp(-c2 m) after choosing C3 universally for c2. Apply the partial-coloring theorem with c2=delta log 2 and repeat on uncolored coordinates. The regular-representation Frobenius identity makes the norm constraint a bounded symmetric convex body, so its hypotheses hold. The remaining sizes decrease geometrically, and monotonicity of x log(e/x) bounds the accumulated discrepancy by a convergent geometric-times-square-root series times sqrt(N). Unitary decomposition then gives simultaneous coverage for arbitrary representation dimension.
finite_matrix_derivations.boundary_checks: No independence of real Fourier blocks is used. Multiplicities repeat blocks without adding constraints. Each round colors at least one coordinate because its required count is a positive fraction of an integer m>=1. The trivial group has discrepancy 1 and is covered by C>=1. The result does not assert a random-sign success probability or efficient construction.

cards.readback: The block-adjoint identity uses Hermitian coefficients. For u=(u_i), the scalar quadratic form is bounded absolutely by the variance via Cauchy–Schwarz and index exchange, and by entry covariance after regrouping coefficients into matrices B_a. The covariance operator is the Gram operator for vec(A_i), so its largest eigenvalue also controls the coefficient map used here. A diagonal block A_i² supplies a nonnegative Rayleigh quotient; this establishes nonnegative largest eigenvalue without asserting C is positive semidefinite. Commutativity turns C into a genuine row Gram matrix, and amplification is permutation-unitarily equivalent to tensoring C with an identity. The distinction between lambda_max(C) and ||C|| is correct.

The source uses normalized trace, agreeing with the explicit tr_d in the card. The Hermite cutoff permits exactly p raising steps from the vacuum; the compressed raising map uses cutoff p−1, giving sigma²+(p−1)kappa². Its symmetric sum has norm at most twice the raising norm. Averaging coordinate vacuum moments gives normalized trace; conversion to ordinary trace contributes d^(1/(2p)). The ceiling choice in Appendix A.2 yields 2sigma+4kappa sqrt(log(2d)); for d≥2 this is bounded by 2sigma+6kappa sqrt(log d). The separate d=1 scalar argument and all-zero-coefficient argument cover the boundaries. No claim about an unbounded operator domain is needed for this finite-degree proof.

Lemma 7 uses exactly independent real and imaginary N(0,1) coordinates, hence E|z|²=2. Schur orthogonality and sum_pi d_pi²=N make the coefficient transform unitary. Its realification preserves the spherical real Gaussian vector in dimension 2N, supplying joint independence of every transformed complex coordinate. Each representation block is scaled by sqrt(N/d_pi), while its d_pi copies are repeated copies of one block, not additional independent matrices. Norm invariance and direct-sum norm yield the maximum identity. Restricting independence to circular complex coefficients correctly avoids the conjugacy constraints present for real coefficients.

The v2 theorem applies to every finite group. The proof explicitly splits at d>(eN/|S|)^4, where the monotonicity of log³(d)/d used in the large-block estimate is justified; the cached v1 cutoff must not be substituted. Gaussian concentration and correlation produce a sufficiently large simultaneous convex constraint set, and the partial-coloring lemma fixes a uniform positive fraction at each stage. The resulting geometric-square-root series is summable with an absolute constant. Control of every irreducible block yields the same signing for every finite-dimensional unitary representation, independent of its multiplicities. This proves existence only, with no random-sign or algorithmic conclusion.

reviews.reason: X†X projects onto (ker X) perpendicular, so Y(I-X†X)=0 is equivalent to ker X contained in ker Y. Sequential reconstruction follows inductively; uniqueness is restricted to range X.

Sylvester determinant identity for B U* and U* B gives the characteristic factor. Both eigenvector transfers require nonzero eigenvalue and nonzero eigenvector; these guards were added to the converse. Projection residual follows by subtracting U U* B w.

Full column/row ranks of O and R make H rank n and T invertible. Multiplication gives O T=U Sigma^(1/2) and T^-1 R=Sigma^(1/2)V*. This proves all three similarity identities and the Hankel-rank lower bound.

Substitute OR V=U Sigma and U*OR=Sigma V* into the three pairings. In the full positive-definite case the biorthogonality identity identifies the inverse. Positive eigenvalues of RR*O*O equal those of ORR*O*, so they are squared positive singular values; an arbitrary PQ eigenbasis is insufficient.

Reviewed the stated scope against the paired Lyapunov energy argument in the source audit: zero initial conditions, finite-horizon inequality with nonnegative storage discarded, one distinct discarded singular value per telescoping step. The uniform bound concerns output error. The transfer-function H-infinity corollary separately assumes both matrices Hurwitz, avoiding an unsupported stability claim.

Orthonormality makes each residual nonzero and interpolation makes its previous selected entries zero; the new pivot is nonzero and extends invertibility. Projection identities follow algebraically. U and P are isometries, giving norm Pi=norm M^-1; the nontrivial oblique-projection norm identity gives the sharp residual factor, with r=n handled separately.

Every off-diagonal entry belongs to exactly one sibling block. At a given depth cluster sizes sum to at most N; dense leaves cost at most Nb. Two directed factor pairs contribute 2k per cluster coordinate. Multiplication and accumulation cost at most twice stored scalar entries.

At a fixed depth, errors are a direct sum of off-diagonal two-by-two blocks; each has norm max(norm E12,norm E21), not their sum. Triangle inequality across depths gives the displayed bound; disjoint matrix entries give the exact Frobenius sum.

source_labels.label: §7.2, Theorem 7.2.1, pp. 799–801; normalized-resolvent proof variant reconstructed independently

meyer.derivation: For rho=0, Cayley–Hamilton makes A nilpotent. If A is nonzero, a nonzero column of the last nonzero power is a nonnegative nullvector; if A=0, use a coordinate vector. For rho>0, scale to rho=1. If 1 were outside the spectrum, the nonnegative resolvent (tI-A)^-1 for t>1 would remain bounded as t decreases to 1. Every finite partial sum of powers is then bounded entrywise by its limiting resolvent bound; monotone convergence forces the Neumann series to converge and hence rho<1, a contradiction. Once 1 is known to be an eigenvalue, the resolvent norm diverges as t decreases to 1. Its entries are nonnegative, so y_t=(tI-A)^-1 1 has unbounded 1-norm. Normalize y_t to the probability simplex and extract a convergent subsequence; dividing (tI-A)y_t=1 by ||y_t||_1 gives Ap=p. This replaces the source spectral-projector limit with a compactness argument but proves the same statement.
meyer.boundary_checks: n=0 is excluded because a normalized nonzero vector cannot exist. The nilpotent matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] is included and shows why rho>0 and strict positivity must not be asserted for arbitrary nonnegative A.

source_labels.label: §7.3, Theorem 7.3.1, pp. 804–805; §7.4, Theorem 7.4.1, Lemma 7.4.2 and Corollary 7.4.4, pp. 809–811

meyer.derivation: For an irreducible nonnegative matrix, the positive weighted sum I+A+...+A^(n-1) is entrywise positive: each directed pair is joined by a simple path of length below n. Thus every resolvent R(t)=(tI-A)^-1 with t>rho(A) is strictly positive, and R(t)p=(t-r)^-1 p makes the nonnegative Perron vectors strictly positive. Nonzero A and positive p give r>0. For a positive matrix, uniqueness of a real Perron eigenvector follows from the extremal-ratio argument: cp-z is nonnegative with a zero coordinate, while its image would be strictly positive if nonzero. Complex eigenvectors split into real and imaginary parts. A generalized eigenvector chain at r cannot exist because a positive left Perron vector annihilates (A-rI) but pairs nontrivially with p. Apply these positive-matrix facts to R(t): its Perron root is (t-r)^-1, and the resolvent spectral mapping preserves algebraic multiplicity at r. Any nonnegative eigenpair has eigenvalue r by pairing with q. Finally P=pq^T/(q^Tp) is idempotent, has range span(p), commutes with A, and kernel range(A-rI), identifying the simple spectral projector.
meyer.boundary_checks: The printed proof of positive-matrix simplicity says a nonzero nonnegative L cannot be nilpotent, which is false in general; its additional relation AL=L with A>0 is needed to make the relevant nonzero columns strictly positive and force a positive diagonal entry. The independent extremal-ratio/Jordan-chain proof above supplies the missing reasoning. A two-cycle permutation matrix is irreducible but has eigenvalues ±1, so no strict peripheral gap is claimed.

meyer.derivation: Induct to obtain |B^k|≤|B|^k≤A^k. Taking the induced infinity norm, kth roots and the Gelfand limit proves rho(B)≤rho(A). This proof does not assume diagonalizability. For the strict variant, A+E remains irreducible. If p>0 is its right Perron vector and q>0 the left Perron vector of A, then (rho(A+E)-rho(A))q^Tp=q^TEp>0. All factors are positive because E has at least one positive entry.
meyer.boundary_checks: Strict comparison fails without irreducibility: A=diag(1,0), E=diag(0,1/2) leave the spectral radius at 1. The zero matrix and nilpotent dominators are covered by the non-strict theorem.

source_labels.label: Theorem 7.3.2, pp. 805–806, and Theorem 7.4.7, p. 817; resolvent proof of the general infimum formula is an audited extension

meyer.derivation: Pair alpha(x)x≤Ax≤beta(x)x with a nonzero nonnegative left Perron vector; its pairing with x>0 is strictly positive, yielding both inequalities. For t>rho(A), x=(tI-A)^-1 1 is strictly positive because the Neumann series includes t^-1 I, and Ax=tx-1, so beta(x)<t. Let t decrease to rho(A), giving the infimum. For irreducible A the positive Perron vector attains both extremal values. For nonzero x≥0 let mu be the minimum ratio on its support; then Ax≥mu x including zero coordinates and mu≥0. Induction gives A^k x≥mu^k x; the induced infinity norm and Gelfand formula imply mu≤rho(A). A nonnegative Perron vector attains equality. This direct comparison proof avoids the spectral-radius continuity argument used in the source.
meyer.boundary_checks: For diag(1,0), alpha(x)=0 for every x>0 although rho=1; hence a blanket positive-vector max-min formula is false. For [[1,1],[0,1]], beta(x)>1 for every x>0, so the general infimum is not attained. No division is performed at a zero coordinate.

source_labels.label: Theorems 7.5.2–7.5.3, pp. 820–821; Exercise 7.5.5(a), p. 823; quantitative geometric rate derived using matrix-power bounds

meyer.derivation: If A^m>0 then A is irreducible. The positive-matrix theorem gives A^m a simple spectral-radius eigenvalue and no other peripheral eigenvalue. Spectral mapping shows that two distinct peripheral eigenvalues of A, or a peripheral nontrivial Jordan chain, would contradict that simplicity. Conversely, irreducible PF already makes r simple; if it is the unique peripheral eigenvalue, B=A/r-P has rho(B)<1, BP=PB=0, and for k≥1, (A/r)^k=P+B^k. Therefore powers converge to P>0, and finitely many entries imply some sufficiently late power is strictly positive. If normalized powers converge, any peripheral scalar lambda/r must have convergent powers, so it equals 1. For x≥0 nonzero, Px is a positive multiple of p and q^TA^kx=r^kq^Tx>0; continuity of normalization proves the power-method limit. Existing matrix-power bounds give the theta rate for k≥1; enlarge the constant to cover k=0.
meyer.boundary_checks: The identity (A/r)^k-P=B^k is not used at k=0: its left side is I-P, while B^0=I. The two-cycle permutation matrix disproves convergence under irreducibility alone. The 1×1 positive case is valid, with zero error after normalization.

source_labels.label: Corollary 4.11.7, Definition 4.11.8 and Theorem 4.11.9, pp. 622–624; Exercise 4.11.14, p. 642

meyer.derivation: If A=sI-B with s>rho(B), the Neumann expansion gives A^-1=(1/s)sum_k(B/s)^k≥0. Conversely choose s≥max_i Aii so B=sI-A≥0. If A is invertible with nonnegative inverse and Bp=rho(B)p for nonnegative nonzero p, then p=(s-rho(B))A^-1p forces s-rho(B)>0. Spectral mapping gives positive stability. Conversely, for a positive-stable Z-matrix choose s larger than every diagonal and every |lambda|^2/(2 Re lambda); then |s-lambda|<s, hence rho(sI-A)<s. Every principal B-block has spectral radius at most rho(B), so principal A-blocks are positive stable and their determinants are positive (positive real eigenvalues and conjugate pairs). For the reverse principal-minor implication use induction and block inversion: the scalar Schur pivot is det(A)/det(E)>0, with E^-1≥0 and off-diagonal blocks nonpositive, so every block of A^-1 is nonnegative. If A^-1≥0, x=A^-1 1 is strictly positive because an invertible nonnegative inverse has no zero row. If Ax>0 for x>0, Bx<sx and the row-ratio certificate gives rho(B)<s. Finally Au≥0 implies u=A^-1Au≥0, and strict row diagonal dominance of A diag(x) is exactly Ax>0.
meyer.boundary_checks: n=1 reduces to a>0. The empty principal determinant is 1 and can be admitted separately. The singular Laplacian [[1,-1],[-1,1]] is weakly diagonally dominant with positive diagonal but not nonsingular; strictness is essential. In the printed induction proof the positivity of the Schur pivot must be justified by the ratio of principal determinants, rather than merely by A being invertible.

source_labels.label: Theorem 4.11.9, (4.11.22)–(4.11.23) and their block-inverse proof, pp. 623–624; Schur-complement equivalence is an audited block-matrix consequence

meyer.derivation: Principal-submatrix closure follows from A=sI-B and nonnegative spectral-radius comparison. Thus if A is an M-matrix, E^-1≥0. Since F,G≤0, GE^-1F≥0 and S=H-GE^-1F is a Z-matrix. Block factorization makes S invertible and gives S^-1 as the lower-right block of A^-1, hence nonnegative. Conversely if E and S are M-matrices, the inverse block formula has diagonal blocks E^-1+E^-1 F S^-1 G E^-1 and S^-1, and off-diagonal blocks -E^-1 F S^-1 and -S^-1 G E^-1. Every block is nonnegative, so A is invertible with nonnegative inverse and therefore an M-matrix.
meyer.boundary_checks: The sign assumptions on F and G follow from A being a Z-matrix, and cannot be discarded. E invertibility is explicit so totalized inverses cannot conceal failed elimination. Empty block partitions reduce to the identity assertion and are omitted from the displayed interface.

Conversely rho(H)<1 gives A^-1=(I-H)^-1M^-1=sum_k H^k M^-1≥0. The existing stationary-splitting theorem supplies convergence for all initializers. For b≥0 and x0=0, x_k=sum_{j=0}^{k-1}H^jM^-1b is an increasing sequence bounded above by the convergent infinite sum A^-1b.

meyer.derivation: Split sum_j omega_n^(kj)x_j into even and odd j. Since omega_n^2=omega_m, the two sums are e_k and omega_n^k o_k. For output k+m, omega_n^m=-1 and periodicity give e_k-omega_n^k o_k. Induction on s proves exact realization of F_n. Each node has m=n/2 butterflies; share the product omega_n^k o_k between its plus and minus outputs, giving m multiplications and n additions/subtractions. The two recursive subproblems yield the displayed recurrences, solved by induction. The base n=1 has no operations. This agrees with the matrix factorization F_n=[[I,D],[I,-D]] diag(F_m,F_m) P_even-odd.

meyer.derivation: For 0≤i<m and 0≤j<n, the difference i-j lies between -(n-1) and m-1. If i≥j, c_(i-j)=t_(j-i); otherwise its residue modulo L is L-(j-i), where the prescribed final segment again gives t_(j-i). The two prescribed nonzero segments do not overlap because L≥m+n-1, including equality. This proves the matrix identity entrywise. Fourier diagonalization of the circulant gives the displayed product. Choose the next power of two L≥m+n-1, so L<2(m+n-1) unless m=n=1; apply the exact FFT recurrence to the forward and inverse transforms. The inverse is conjugation of a forward transform followed by 1/L scaling, contributing only O(L) additional arithmetic.
meyer.boundary_checks: The minimal length m+n-1 is valid. Shorter padding can alias distinct Toeplitz diagonals and is not claimed. The m=n=1 endpoint reduces to scalar multiplication. Extracting the leading block of a circulant inverse is generally not the inverse of its Toeplitz leading block.

baseline_audit.informal: Every entrywise nonnegative real square matrix has a nonnegative eigenvector for its spectral radius. This includes reducible matrices and the zero spectral-radius case.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and $A_{ij}\ge0$ for every $i,j$; $\rho(A)$ is the spectral radius of the complexification
baseline_audit.conclusion: There is $p\ge0$ with $\sum_i p_i=1$ and $Ap=\rho(A)p$. The transpose gives a normalized nonnegative left eigenvector as well.
baseline_audit.notes: All matrix and vector inequalities here are entrywise. Neither positivity of every coordinate, simplicity, nor a spectral gap follows without additional hypotheses. Reuse the existing complexified spectral-radius and Neumann-series API.

source_labels.label: §7.2, Theorem 7.2.1, pp. 799–801; normalized-resolvent proof variant reconstructed independently

records.readback: For rho=0, Cayley–Hamilton makes A nilpotent. If A is nonzero, a nonzero column of the last nonzero power is a nonnegative nullvector; if A=0, use a coordinate vector. For rho>0, scale to rho=1. If 1 were outside the spectrum, the nonnegative resolvent (tI-A)^-1 for t>1 would remain bounded as t decreases to 1. Every finite partial sum of powers is then bounded entrywise by its limiting resolvent bound; monotone convergence forces the Neumann series to converge and hence rho<1, a contradiction. Once 1 is known to be an eigenvalue, the resolvent norm diverges as t decreases to 1. Its entries are nonnegative, so y_t=(tI-A)^-1 1 has unbounded 1-norm. Normalize y_t to the probability simplex and extract a convergent subsequence; dividing (tI-A)y_t=1 by ||y_t||_1 gives Ap=p. This replaces the source spectral-projector limit with a compactness argument but proves the same statement. Boundary and counterexample checks: n=0 is excluded because a normalized nonzero vector cannot exist. The nilpotent matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] is included and shows why rho>0 and strict positivity must not be asserted for arbitrary nonnegative A.

baseline_audit.informal: An irreducible nonnegative matrix has strictly positive right and left Perron vectors and an algebraically simple Perron root. Its Perron spectral projector is positive and explicitly rank one.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, is entrywise nonnegative, nonzero and irreducible (its directed support graph is strongly connected)
$r=\rho(A)$; normalize right and left Perron vectors by $\sum_i p_i=\sum_i q_i=1$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $r>0$, $p,q>0$, $Ap=rp$, $A^\top q=rq$, and $r$ has algebraic multiplicity one. Every nonzero nonnegative eigenvector is a positive multiple of the corresponding Perron vector. The spectral projector at $r$ is $P=pq^\top/(q^\top p)>0$.
baseline_audit.notes: The nonzero assumption handles the 1×1 zero matrix under the usual graph-theoretic irreducibility convention. Irreducibility does not exclude other eigenvalues on the spectral circle; primitivity is a separate condition. The projector is generally oblique.

source_labels.label: §7.3, Theorem 7.3.1, pp. 804–805; §7.4, Theorem 7.4.1, Lemma 7.4.2 and Corollary 7.4.4, pp. 809–811

records.readback: For an irreducible nonnegative matrix, the positive weighted sum I+A+...+A^(n-1) is entrywise positive: each directed pair is joined by a simple path of length below n. Thus every resolvent R(t)=(tI-A)^-1 with t>rho(A) is strictly positive, and R(t)p=(t-r)^-1 p makes the nonnegative Perron vectors strictly positive. Nonzero A and positive p give r>0. For a positive matrix, uniqueness of a real Perron eigenvector follows from the extremal-ratio argument: cp-z is nonnegative with a zero coordinate, while its image would be strictly positive if nonzero. Complex eigenvectors split into real and imaginary parts. A generalized eigenvector chain at r cannot exist because a positive left Perron vector annihilates (A-rI) but pairs nontrivially with p. Apply these positive-matrix facts to R(t): its Perron root is (t-r)^-1, and the resolvent spectral mapping preserves algebraic multiplicity at r. Any nonnegative eigenpair has eigenvalue r by pairing with q. Finally P=pq^T/(q^Tp) is idempotent, has range span(p), commutes with A, and kernel range(A-rI), identifying the simple spectral projector. Boundary and counterexample checks: The printed proof of positive-matrix simplicity says a nonzero nonnegative L cannot be nilpotent, which is false in general; its additional relation AL=L with A>0 is needed to make the relevant nonzero columns strictly positive and force a positive diagonal entry. The independent extremal-ratio/Jordan-chain proof above supplies the missing reasoning. A two-cycle permutation matrix is irreducible but has eigenvalues ±1, so no strict peripheral gap is claimed.

baseline_audit.informal: Entrywise absolute-value domination controls spectral radii even for a complex matrix. A nonzero entrywise increase strictly raises the spectral radius when the smaller nonnegative matrix is irreducible.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, is entrywise nonnegative; $B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $|B_{ij}|\le A_{ij}$
For the strict variant, $A$ is nonzero and irreducible, $E\ge0$ entrywise and $E\ne0$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\rho(B)\le\rho(A)$. In the strict variant, $\rho(A+E)>\rho(A)$. In particular $0\le A\le C$ entrywise implies $\rho(A)\le\rho(C)$.
baseline_audit.notes: Entrywise order must not be confused with Loewner order. No corresponding monotonicity of spectral radius for arbitrary signed entrywise-ordered matrices is asserted.

records.readback: Induct to obtain |B^k|≤|B|^k≤A^k. Taking the induced infinity norm, kth roots and the Gelfand limit proves rho(B)≤rho(A). This proof does not assume diagonalizability. For the strict variant, A+E remains irreducible. If p>0 is its right Perron vector and q>0 the left Perron vector of A, then (rho(A+E)-rho(A))q^Tp=q^TEp>0. All factors are positive because E has at least one positive entry. Boundary and counterexample checks: Strict comparison fails without irreducibility: A=diag(1,0), E=diag(0,1/2) leave the spectral radius at 1. The zero matrix and nilpotent dominators are covered by the non-strict theorem.

baseline_audit.informal: Positive test vectors give certified lower and upper bounds for a nonnegative matrix’s spectral radius. For irreducible matrices both bounds are attained at the Perron vector; reducible matrices require care about the domain and attainment.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, is entrywise nonnegative
$\alpha(x)=\min_i(Ax)_i/x_i$ and $\beta(x)=\max_i(Ax)_i/x_i$ for $x>0$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\alpha(x)\le\rho(A)\le\beta(x)$ for every $x>0$, and $\rho(A)=\inf_{x>0}\beta(x)$. If $A$ is irreducible and nonzero, $\rho(A)=\min_{x>0}\beta(x)=\max_{x>0}\alpha(x)$. For arbitrary $A\ge0$, the support-aware formula is $\rho(A)=\max_{0\ne x\ge0}\min_{i:x_i>0}(Ax)_i/x_i$.
baseline_audit.notes: Each minimum over coordinates is over a nonempty finite set. Reducible matrices need not have a positive Perron vector, so the upper infimum need not be a minimum and the positive-vector max-min need not equal the spectral radius. This is a useful a posteriori certificate for Perron iterations.

records.readback: Pair alpha(x)x≤Ax≤beta(x)x with a nonzero nonnegative left Perron vector; its pairing with x>0 is strictly positive, yielding both inequalities. For t>rho(A), x=(tI-A)^-1 1 is strictly positive because the Neumann series includes t^-1 I, and Ax=tx-1, so beta(x)<t. Let t decrease to rho(A), giving the infimum. For irreducible A the positive Perron vector attains both extremal values. For nonzero x≥0 let mu be the minimum ratio on its support; then Ax≥mu x including zero coordinates and mu≥0. Induction gives A^k x≥mu^k x; the induced infinity norm and Gelfand formula imply mu≤rho(A). A nonnegative Perron vector attains equality. This direct comparison proof avoids the spectral-radius continuity argument used in the source. Boundary and counterexample checks: For diag(1,0), alpha(x)=0 for every x>0 although rho=1; hence a blanket positive-vector max-min formula is false. For [[1,1],[0,1]], beta(x)>1 for every x>0, so the general infimum is not attained. No division is performed at a zero coordinate.

baseline_audit.informal: Primitivity is exactly the missing hypothesis that turns irreducible Perron theory into convergence of normalized powers and the nonnegative power method.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, is entrywise nonnegative, nonzero and irreducible; $r=\rho(A)$
$p,q>0$ are Perron vectors and $\sum_i p_i=1$; $P=pq^\top/(q^\top p)$
baseline_audit.conclusion: The following are equivalent: some $A^m$ with $m\ge1$ is entrywise positive; $r$ is the only eigenvalue of modulus $r$; and $(A/r)^k$ converges. In this case $(A/r)^k\to P$. For every $0\ne x\ge0$, $A^kx/\sum_i(A^kx)_i\to p$. If $\theta$ is strictly between $\rho(A/r-P)$ and $1$, then $\|(A/r)^k-P\|_2\le C_\theta\theta^k$ for all $k\ge0$ and some finite $C_\theta$.
baseline_audit.notes: The geometric estimate uses any rate strictly larger than the subdominant spectral radius and permits a nontrivial prefactor. A defective subdominant eigenvalue prevents an unqualified exact-ratio rate. All normalization denominators are positive for nonzero nonnegative initial vectors.

source_labels.label: Theorems 7.5.2–7.5.3, pp. 820–821; Exercise 7.5.5(a), p. 823; quantitative geometric rate derived using matrix-power bounds

records.readback: If A^m>0 then A is irreducible. The positive-matrix theorem gives A^m a simple spectral-radius eigenvalue and no other peripheral eigenvalue. Spectral mapping shows that two distinct peripheral eigenvalues of A, or a peripheral nontrivial Jordan chain, would contradict that simplicity. Conversely, irreducible PF already makes r simple; if it is the unique peripheral eigenvalue, B=A/r-P has rho(B)<1, BP=PB=0, and for k≥1, (A/r)^k=P+B^k. Therefore powers converge to P>0, and finitely many entries imply some sufficiently late power is strictly positive. If normalized powers converge, any peripheral scalar lambda/r must have convergent powers, so it equals 1. For x≥0 nonzero, Px is a positive multiple of p and q^TA^kx=r^kq^Tx>0; continuity of normalization proves the power-method limit. Existing matrix-power bounds give the theta rate for k≥1; enlarge the constant to cover k=0. Boundary and counterexample checks: The identity (A/r)^k-P=B^k is not used at k=0: its left side is I-P, while B^0=I. The two-cycle permutation matrix disproves convergence under irreducibility alone. The 1×1 positive case is valid, with zero error after normalization.

baseline_audit.informal: For a real Z-matrix, nonsingular M-matrix structure can be recognized spectrally, through its inverse or principal minors, or by a positive vector certificate. These characterizations support monotone linear solves and convergent splittings.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, is a Z-matrix: $A_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$
baseline_audit.conclusion: The following are equivalent: $A$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\ge0$ entrywise; $A=sI-B$ with $B\ge0$ and $s>\rho(B)$; every eigenvalue of $A$ has positive real part; all nonempty principal minors are positive; and there exists $x>0$ with $Ax>0$. The last condition is equivalently strict row diagonal dominance of $A\operatorname{diag}(x)$ with positive diagonal. Such $A$ satisfies $Au\ge0\Rightarrow u\ge0$.
baseline_audit.notes: Meyer uses M-matrix to mean nonsingular M-matrix; the title makes this convention explicit because other sources permit singular M-matrices. Positivity and inequalities are entrywise. The positive-scaling criterion is strict diagonal dominance, not an unqualified weak-dominance test.

source_labels.label: Corollary 4.11.7, Definition 4.11.8 and Theorem 4.11.9, pp. 622–624; Exercise 4.11.14, p. 642

records.readback: If A=sI-B with s>rho(B), the Neumann expansion gives A^-1=(1/s)sum_k(B/s)^k≥0. Conversely choose s≥max_i Aii so B=sI-A≥0. If A is invertible with nonnegative inverse and Bp=rho(B)p for nonnegative nonzero p, then p=(s-rho(B))A^-1p forces s-rho(B)>0. Spectral mapping gives positive stability. Conversely, for a positive-stable Z-matrix choose s larger than every diagonal and every |lambda|^2/(2 Re lambda); then |s-lambda|<s, hence rho(sI-A)<s. Every principal B-block has spectral radius at most rho(B), so principal A-blocks are positive stable and their determinants are positive (positive real eigenvalues and conjugate pairs). For the reverse principal-minor implication use induction and block inversion: the scalar Schur pivot is det(A)/det(E)>0, with E^-1≥0 and off-diagonal blocks nonpositive, so every block of A^-1 is nonnegative. If A^-1≥0, x=A^-1 1 is strictly positive because an invertible nonnegative inverse has no zero row. If Ax>0 for x>0, Bx<sx and the row-ratio certificate gives rho(B)<s. Finally Au≥0 implies u=A^-1Au≥0, and strict row diagonal dominance of A diag(x) is exactly Ax>0. Boundary and counterexample checks: n=1 reduces to a>0. The empty principal determinant is 1 and can be admitted separately. The singular Laplacian [[1,-1],[-1,1]] is weakly diagonally dominant with positive diagonal but not nonsingular; strictness is essential. In the printed induction proof the positivity of the Schur pivot must be justified by the ratio of principal determinants, rather than merely by A being invertible.

baseline_audit.informal: Every principal submatrix and every principal Schur complement of a nonsingular M-matrix is again a nonsingular M-matrix. The converse block criterion explains why elimination preserves inverse positivity.
hypotheses: $A=\begin{pmatrix}E&F\\G&H\end{pmatrix}$ is a real Z-matrix with two nonempty principal blocks
For the Schur-complement equivalence assume $E$ is invertible and put $S=H-GE^{-1}F$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $A$ is a nonsingular M-matrix iff both $E$ and $S$ are nonsingular M-matrices. In the forward direction every nonempty principal submatrix of $A$ is also a nonsingular M-matrix, and $S^{-1}$ is the bottom-right principal block of $A^{-1}$.
baseline_audit.notes: This is an entrywise inverse-positivity theorem for generally nonsymmetric matrices; it is distinct from the existing PSD Schur-complement theorem. Rectangular off-diagonal blocks are allowed, and no symmetry is assumed.

source_labels.label: Theorem 4.11.9, (4.11.22)–(4.11.23) and their block-inverse proof, pp. 623–624; Schur-complement equivalence is an audited block-matrix consequence

records.readback: Principal-submatrix closure follows from A=sI-B and nonnegative spectral-radius comparison. Thus if A is an M-matrix, E^-1≥0. Since F,G≤0, GE^-1F≥0 and S=H-GE^-1F is a Z-matrix. Block factorization makes S invertible and gives S^-1 as the lower-right block of A^-1, hence nonnegative. Conversely if E and S are M-matrices, the inverse block formula has diagonal blocks E^-1+E^-1 F S^-1 G E^-1 and S^-1, and off-diagonal blocks -E^-1 F S^-1 and -S^-1 G E^-1. Every block is nonnegative, so A is invertible with nonnegative inverse and therefore an M-matrix. Boundary and counterexample checks: The sign assumptions on F and G follow from A being a Z-matrix, and cannot be discarded. E invertibility is explicit so totalized inverses cannot conceal failed elimination. Empty block partitions reduce to the identity assertion and are omitted from the displayed interface.

baseline_audit.informal: A regular splitting converts inverse positivity into a spectral-radius convergence certificate. Consequently every regular splitting of a nonsingular M-matrix converges, and nonnegative data give a monotone iteration from zero.
hypotheses: $A=M-N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, $M$ invertible, $M^{-1}\ge0$ and $N\ge0$ entrywise
baseline_audit.conclusion: $A$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\ge0$ iff $\rho(H)<1$. Under these conditions the iteration converges to $A^{-1}b$ for every $b,x_0$. If $b\ge0$ and $x_0=0$, then $0\le x_k\le x_{k+1}\le A^{-1}b$.
baseline_audit.notes: The printed (4.11.24) statement omits N≥0, although its proof uses it. Both M^-1≥0 and N≥0 are required here. No Z-matrix assumption on A is needed for the equivalence itself; M-matrix structure is one sufficient certificate of inverse positivity.

records.readback: H≥0. If A is inverse-positive, I-H=M^-1A is invertible and (I-H)^-1=A^-1M=I+A^-1N≥0; the nonsingular M-matrix characterization of I-H therefore gives rho(H)<1. Conversely rho(H)<1 gives A^-1=(I-H)^-1M^-1=sum_k H^k M^-1≥0. The existing stationary-splitting theorem supplies convergence for all initializers. For b≥0 and x0=0, x_k=sum_{j=0}^{k-1}H^jM^-1b is an increasing sequence bounded above by the convergent infinite sum A^-1b. Boundary and counterexample checks: A=1, M=1/3, N=-2/3 gives an M-matrix A and M^-1>0 but H=-2, disproving the printed version without N≥0. If N=0 then H=0 and the iteration reaches the solution in one step. Neither floating-point monotonicity nor convergence of irregular splittings is asserted.

baseline_audit.informal: The normalized DFT simultaneously diagonalizes all circulant matrices. Their singular values, spectral norm and invertibility are therefore read directly from the Fourier transform of their first column.
hypotheses: $n\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z}$, and $C_{ij}=c_{i-j}$
$F_{jk}=e^{-2\pi i jk/n}$, $U=F/\sqrt n$, and $\widehat c=Fc$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $U$ is unitary and $UCU^*=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat c)$. The singular-value multiset of $C$ is $\{|\widehat c_j|:0\le j<n\}$, $\|C\|_2=\max_j|\widehat c_j|$, and $C$ is invertible iff every $\widehat c_j\ne0$. In that case $\kappa_2(C)=\max_j|\widehat c_j|/\min_j|\widehat c_j|$.
baseline_audit.notes: Use Mathlib’s ZMod.dft and Matrix.circulant rather than introducing duplicate foundational objects. The normalized unitary U and unnormalized transform F must be distinguished: the diagonal entries are Fc, not Uc. Singular values are a multiset before sorting.

records.readback: The finite geometric sum gives FF*=nI, including n=1. Writing l=i-j in (FC)_{kj} gives sum_l omega^(k(l+j))c_l=(Fc)_k F_kj, hence FC=diag(Fc)F. Divide by sqrt(n) and multiply by U* to obtain the unitary diagonalization. Consequently C*C is unitarily similar to diag(|Fc|^2), giving its singular values. The spectral norm is their maximum, invertibility excludes zero Fourier coefficients, and the inverse has singular values 1/|Fc|; their product gives the condition number. Boundary and counterexample checks: Checked the first-column convention Cij=c(i-j) and the negative Fourier sign against the pinned Mathlib source. For n=1, F=U=[1]. At a zero Fourier coefficient C is singular, so the ordinary condition number is infinity and the displayed finite ratio is not used.

baseline_audit.informal: Fourier coordinates reduce a circulant linear solve or least-squares problem to independent scalar divisions. Setting reciprocal zero modes to zero gives the Moore–Penrose inverse and the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
hypotheses: $n\ge1$, $C=\operatorname{circulant}(c)\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$; $F_{jk}=e^{-2\pi i jk/n}$, $U=F/\sqrt n$, $\lambda=Fc$
$d_j=\lambda_j^{-1}$ when $\lambda_j\ne0$, and $d_j=0$ otherwise; $b\in\mathbb C^n$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $C^+=U^*\operatorname{diag}(d)U=\operatorname{circulant}(F^{-1}d)$. The minimum-norm least-squares solution is $x_*=F^{-1}(d\odot Fb)$. Its squared residual is $\sum_{j:\lambda_j=0}|(Ub)_j|^2$, and $Cx=b$ is solvable iff $(Fb)_j=0$ at every zero mode. If every mode is nonzero, this is the unique exact solution.
baseline_audit.notes: The source exercise assumes nonsingularity. The pseudoinverse and residual formulas here are explicit audited extensions, obtained by applying the existing Moore–Penrose API to a diagonal matrix. They do not reinterpret a totalized matrix inverse as the pseudoinverse.

baseline_audit.informal: The even–odd butterfly recurrence computes the existing DFT exactly. For a length $2^s$ input it uses at most $(n/2)s$ complex multiplications and $ns$ complex additions/subtractions, when roots of unity are supplied as constants.
hypotheses: $s\in\mathbb N$, $n=2^s$, $x\in\mathbb C^n$, and $\omega_n=e^{-2\pi i/n}$

For $n=1$ return $x$; for $n=2m$, recursively compute $e=\operatorname{FFT}_m(x_{2j})$ and $o=\operatorname{FFT}_m(x_{2j+1})$, then return $y_k=e_k+\omega_n^k o_k$ and $y_{k+m}=e_k-\omega_n^k o_k$ for $0\le k<m$
baseline_audit.conclusion: This recurrence returns $F_nx$, with $F_{jk}=\omega_n^{jk}$. Counting one supplied-constant multiplication per butterfly and two additions/subtractions gives $M_0=A_0=0$, $M_s=2M_{s-1}+2^{s-1}$ and $A_s=2A_{s-1}+2^s$, hence $M_s=s2^{s-1}$ for $s\ge1$ and $A_s=s2^s$. Multiplication by trivial roots may be omitted, so these are upper bounds for an optimized implementation.
baseline_audit.notes: Exact complex arithmetic only. Roots are supplied or precomputed; indexing/permutation, twiddle generation, memory movement and bit complexity are outside the counted operations. This is an algorithm-to-specification bridge, not just a Fourier factorization or a wall-clock speed claim.

$0<\ell<1$ and every nonzero singular value of $A$ belongs to $[\ell,1]$; $d=2q+1$ with $q\ge1$ and $T\ge1$

records.readback: The regular representation decomposes as U direct_sum_pi(I_dpi tensor pi(g)) U*. Schur orthogonality makes the coefficient map a_g -> (sqrt(dpi/N) sum_g a_g pi(g)_{ij})_(pi,i,j) unitary; the dimension identity sum dpi²=N makes it square. A circular complex Gaussian vector is invariant under this unitary map, as its realification is orthogonal on 2N independent standard real coordinates. Its output coordinates are jointly independent circular Gaussians, giving each block scaling sqrt(N/dpi) and multiplicity dpi. Spectral norm is unchanged by U and is the maximum of the block norms; repeated copies do not introduce additional independent randomness. This exact law is the reusable matrix-method core; the simple-group norm corollaries rely on separate classification and dimension estimates and were not re-audited. In covariance language the normalized Fourier vector has covariance 2I and pseudocovariance zero. Both facts are needed for independent circular complex coordinates. With real coefficients, covariance alone is insufficient; conjugate irreducibles can produce conjugate blocks. The repeated I_dpi tensor copies are exactly equal copies of one random block, not independent copies.

records.readback: For a subset S and irreducible block pi of dimension d, unitarity gives variance |S|, Schur orthogonality gives entry-covariance <=N/d, and the scalar Gaussian Lipschitz variance is <=|S|. Low-dimensional blocks use noncommutative Khintchine. For d>(eN/|S|)^4, intrinsic-freeness concentration gives expected norm O(sqrt|S|); log³(d)/d is decreasing in this range because d>e^4. This is the corrected v2 threshold; v1 used power 2, where the monotonicity step is not justified. Gaussian concentration gives each block an arbitrarily small power-law failure in eN/|S|. The norm constraints are centrally symmetric convex sets, so the Gaussian correlation inequality yields joint mass at least exp(-c|S|), with c chosen for the partial-coloring lemma. Iterated partial coloring fixes a uniform positive fraction of remaining signs at each round. The accumulated bound is C sqrt(N) sum_t sqrt((1-delta)^t(1+t log(1/(1-delta)))), a convergent series independent of N. Finally every unitary representation decomposes into the already controlled irreducibles, proving simultaneous coverage. Hermitian dilation supplies the nonselfadjoint Gaussian block comparison, with universal factors absorbed in C. The external Gaussian correlation and partial-coloring theorems were checked as explicit prerequisite statements, not reproved in this screening. More explicitly, write r=N/|S|>=1 and q=er. The high-dimensional term is bounded using f(d)=log(d)^3/d, whose derivative is log(d)^2(3-log(d))/d^2<0 for d>e^3; the v2 cutoff d>q^4>=e^4 lies in that range. For C3>=max(1,log 2), the number of irreducibles is at most N and 2 sum_pi p_pi/|S| <=2e^(-C3)(|S|/N)^(C3-1), which can be made <=delta log 2 for partial coloring. The norm constraint is a genuine convex body on R^S: regular-representation orthogonality gives ||sum_g x_g rho(g)||_F^2=N||x||_2^2, hence its spectral norm is at least ||x||_2, ensuring boundedness. Real block events are correlated; their independence is never used. The N=1 case has norm 1 and is covered by enlarging the universal constant.

hypotheses: $d \ge 2q+1$
